lessons.title: Compare Lengths
lessons.explanation: Compare object lengths directly by aligning their starting endpoints and describing which extends farther. Order three objects shortest to longest.
lessons.examples: Example 1: A strip starts at the same line as another strip. The red strip ends after the blue one, so red is longer. Example 2: 5 cubes, 7 cubes, 9 cubes ordered by identical unit are shortest to longest.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Put one end of each object at the same starting line. Step 2: Compare where the other ends stop. Step 3: Order three objects. Step 4: Describe 'shorter than' or 'longer than'.
lessons.mistakes: Do not compare objects from different starting positions or confuse the number of objects with their length.
lessons.summary: I can compare and order lengths by aligning starting points.

lessons.title: Center Day 1
lessons.explanation: Choose between teacher-led within-100 addition games and within-20 number-expression comparisons. Only numeric answers are digitally checked; live center turns require a teacher.
lessons.examples: Example 1: 35+24=59 using tens and ones. Example 2: 8+7=15 and 18-3=15, so those expressions are equal.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Identify whether the center requires a within-100 sum or comparison of within-20 expressions. Step 2: Select a matching method. Step 3: Solve both sides if comparing. Step 4: Explain the reasoning.
lessons.mistakes: Do not compare 8+7 and 18-3 as strings or infer equality from matching operation signs.
lessons.summary: I can add within 100 and compare the values of expressions in center work.

lessons.title: Measure with Paper Clips
lessons.explanation: Measure object length by placing paper clips end to end. The clips must be equally long and leave no gaps or overlaps; record the count with unit name.
lessons.examples: Example 1: A pencil spans 8 equally sized paper clips in a continuous row, so it is 8 paper clips long. Example 2: Four short clips cannot be compared directly with four long clips as equal lengths.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Choose same-size paper clips. Step 2: Put first clip at the object's start. Step 3: Place others end-to-end with no gaps or overlap. Step 4: Count the clips and record the unit.
lessons.mistakes: Do not leave spaces, overlap clips, or mix clip lengths and then trust the count as a length.
lessons.summary: I can measure an object accurately with repeated identical paper clips.

lessons.title: Measure Length with Different Length Units
lessons.explanation: Measure the SAME object using different size units and explain why the numerical count changes while actual length stays the same.
lessons.examples: Example 1: A strip measures 6 short blocks but 3 double-length blocks; the strip did not change. Example 2: 4 equal paper clips may cover the same length as 8 half-length units.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Measure an object with repeated equal small units. Step 2: Repeat with a different unit length. Step 3: Record both numbers AND unit names. Step 4: Compare how unit size affects the count.
lessons.mistakes: Do not conclude that the object became longer merely because the count using smaller units increased.
lessons.summary: I can explain how choice of length unit changes the number in a measurement.

lessons.title: Groups Up to 110 PLC Activity
lessons.explanation: PLC: measure a long length in equal cube lengths, then organize those counted units into full tens to read a total up to 110. Teacher discussion remains teacher-led.
lessons.examples: Example 1: 8 full groups of ten cubes and 6 extra cubes total 86 units. Example 2: 10 groups of ten and 7 loose units total 107.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Lay cubes in a continuous length with no gaps. Step 2: Count the equal cube units. Step 3: Bundle counts of ten to avoid losing track. Step 4: Read the final count up to 110.
lessons.mistakes: Do not count a gap as a cube unit or read 10 tens and 7 ones as 17.
lessons.summary: I can group and read up to 110 equal length units.

lessons.title: Write Numbers to 120
lessons.explanation: Count to and write numbers as high as 120 while measuring lengths in equal units. Model 100 as ten tens and distinguish 111 from 101.
lessons.examples: Example 1: After 99 come 100, 101, 102. Example 2: Eleven tens and 4 ones make 114, which is less than 120. Example 3: A length of 103 cubes is 100 plus three equal cube units.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Count by tens to a useful landmark. Step 2: Add leftover ones without skipping. Step 3: Say and write the number up to 120. Step 4: Check digits and unit count.
lessons.mistakes: Do not write 110 as 101 or jump from 109 to 200. Numbers from 100 through 120 have three digits.
lessons.summary: I can read and write counts and measurements through 120.

lessons.title: Center Day 2
lessons.explanation: Teacher-led center: add within 100 and measure with same-size length units placed without gaps or overlaps. These are separate center objectives.
lessons.examples: Example 1: 36+25=61 using tens and ones. Example 2: A line covered by 9 equal connecting cubes measures 9 cube-length units.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Read which center task is selected. Step 2: For addition, combine tens/ones and regroup when needed. Step 3: For measurement, tile equal units with no gaps. Step 4: Check the answer and name the units.
lessons.mistakes: Do not substitute arithmetic for actual measurement, or count units of mixed sizes as though they are interchangeable.
lessons.summary: I can add or measure accurately in an appropriate teacher-led center.

lessons.title: Compare Measurements
lessons.explanation: Compare measurements and solve a Difference Unknown story. Both lengths must be expressed using the SAME unit to compare counts directly.
lessons.examples: Example 1: A ribbon is 14 cubes long and another is 9 cubes long. The first is 5 cubes longer because 14-9=5. Example 2: A 12-clip strip is 3 clips shorter than a 15-clip strip.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Confirm the measurements use the same unit. Step 2: Identify longer and shorter objects. Step 3: Subtract shorter count from longer count. Step 4: Express the difference with the unit.
lessons.mistakes: Do not subtract counts expressed in different unit sizes without first accounting for the unit; do not confuse total with difference.
lessons.summary: I can compare lengths and explain how much longer or shorter one is.

lessons.title: Solve Take From Story Problems
lessons.explanation: Solve Take From stories with unknown starting amount, amount removed, or amount left. Use counters and related addition/subtraction.
lessons.examples: Example 1: There were 16 cubes, 7 were taken, 9 remain: 16-7=9. Example 2: 15 were present, some taken, 6 remain: 15-□=6, so 9 taken. Example 3: Some cubes present, 4 taken, 8 remain: □-4=8, so 12 originally.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Identify the story's original total, removed amount and remaining amount. Step 2: Place the unknown correctly. Step 3: Solve using a model or related fact. Step 4: Check the story.
lessons.mistakes: Do not assume every subtraction question asks for the amount left; unknowns can occur in any position.
lessons.summary: I can solve Take From stories with the unknown in different positions.

lessons.title: Which Equation Matches? PLC Activity
lessons.explanation: PLC: match addition or subtraction equations to realistic stories, including unknowns in all positions. Discuss WHY an equation represents the story.
lessons.examples: Example 1: 12 birds, 5 fly away, 7 left corresponds to 12-5=7. Example 2: 7 birds present and 5 join corresponds to 7+5=12. Example 3: 12 present and some depart leaving 7 corresponds to 12-□=7.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Identify what changes in the situation. Step 2: Name the known numbers and unknown. Step 3: Match operation and blank position. Step 4: Check the proposed equation is true for the story.
lessons.mistakes: Do not choose addition for a leaving story simply because it contains the same numbers, unless using inverse addition to solve a missing value.
lessons.summary: I can explain which equation matches a story and where its unknown belongs.

lessons.title: Write Equations for Story Problems
lessons.explanation: Write, not just select, an addition or subtraction equation matching a story with a missing start, change, or result.
lessons.examples: Example 1: Nine people, five join: 9+5=14. Example 2: □ children plus 6 children makes 13, so □+6=13 and □=7. Example 3: 17-□=8, so 9 left.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Read the whole story before calculating. Step 2: Draw or describe its quantities. Step 3: Put the box in the correct equation position. Step 4: Find the unknown and verify the equation matches the story.
lessons.mistakes: Do not always place □ at the end. In □+6=13 the unknown START equals 7, not 19.
lessons.summary: I can write accurate equations for different addition/subtraction stories.

lessons.title: Center Day 3
lessons.explanation: Center review includes counting collections through 120, measuring with equal units, and addition within 100. Physical measurement and classroom turns remain teacher-facilitated.
lessons.examples: Example 1: 9 tens and 5 ones represent 95 objects. Example 2: 42+37=79. Example 3: a strip measuring 8 identical cubes is 8 cube lengths.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Identify which center objective the task actually uses. Step 2: Count tens/ones, measure equal units, or add two numbers as appropriate. Step 3: Record quantity, units or equation. Step 4: Verify.
lessons.mistakes: Do not automatically certify paper-and-cube measurement from a digital numerical answer or omit the unit.
lessons.summary: I can choose accurate counting, measuring, and adding strategies for center tasks.
